local action of the companion paper, establishing locality as the short-memory limit of a nonlocal
theory. We verify the reversible sector of this expansion term by term against an exactly solvable
vector linear model.

Foundation models, now powering most of the exciting applications in deep learning, are almost universally based on the
Transformer architecture and its core attention module. Many subquadratic-time architectures such as linear attention,
gated convolution and recurrent models, and structured state space models (SSMs) have been developed to address
Transformers’ computational inefficiency on long sequences, but they have not performed as well as attention on important
modalities such as language. We identify that a key weakness of such models is their inability to perform content-based
reasoning, and make several improvements. First, simply letting the SSM parameters be functions of the input addresses
their weakness with discrete modalities, allowing the model to selectively propagate or forget information along the
sequence length dimension depending on the current token. Second, even though this change prevents the use of efficient
convolutions, we design a hardware-aware parallel algorithm in recurrent mode. We integrate these selective SSMs into a
simplified end-to-end neural network architecture without attention or even MLP blocks (Mamba). Mamba enjoys fast
inference (5× higher throughput than Transformers) and linear scaling in sequence length, and its performance improves
on real data up to million-length sequences. As a general sequence model backbone, Mamba achieves state-of-the-art
performance across several modalities such as language, audio, and genomics. On language modeling, our Mamba-3B model
outperforms Transformers of the same size and matches Transformers twice its size, both in pretraining and downstream
evaluation.

General State Space Models.
We note that the term state space model has a very broad meaning which simply represents
the notion of any recurrent process with a latent state. It has been used to refer to many disparate concepts in different
disciplines, including Markov decision processes (MDP) (reinforcement learning (Hafner et al. 2020)), dynamic causal
modeling (DCM) (computational neuroscience (Friston, Harrison, and Penny 2003)), Kalman filters (controls (Kalman 1960)),
hidden Markov models (HMM) and linear dynamical systems (LDS) (machine learning), and recurrent (and sometimes
convolutional) models at large (deep learning).

Table 11: (Induction heads.) Models are trained on sequence length 28 = 256, and tested on various sequence lengths of 26 = 64 up to
220 = 1048576. ✓denotes perfect generalization accuracy, while ✗denotes out of memory.

Figure 5: (DNA Scaling Laws.) Pretraining on the HG38 (human genome) dataset. (Left) Fixing short context length 210 = 1024 and
increasing size from ≈200𝐾to ≈40𝑀parameters, Mamba scales better than baselines. (Right) Fixing model size and increasing sequence
lengths while keeping tokens/batch and total training tokens fixed. Unlike baselines, the selection mechanism of Mamba facilitates
better performance with increasing context length.

Induction heads (Olsson et al. 2022) is a simple task from the mechanistic interpretability lens (Elhage et al. 2021) that is
surprisingly predictive of the in-context learning ability of LLMs. It requires models to perform associative recall and copy:
for example, if the model has seen a bigram such as “Harry Potter” in the sequence, then the next time “Harry” appears in
the same sequence, the model should be able to predict “Potter” by copying from history.

We motivate our selection mechanism using intuition from synthetic tasks (Section 3.1), then explain how to incorporate
this mechanism into state space models (Section 3.2). The resulting time-varying SSMs cannot use convolutions, presenting
a technical challenge of how to compute them efficiently. We overcome this with a hardware-aware algorithm that exploits
the memory hierarchy on modern hardware (Section 3.3). We then describe a simple SSM architecture without attention or
even MLP blocks (Section 3.4). Finally, we discuss some additional properties of selection mechanisms (Section 3.5).

is introduced in Sec. II. Sec. III then presents the kinetic theory framework to describe the statistics of a spatially
homogeneous assembly of learning agents. This microscopic theory in then reduced in Sec. IV to derive a macroscopic
statistical description of the decentralized learning dynamics characterized by the time evolution of the policy distribu-

of closure approximations, which are discussed in Sec. IV C. Two applications to explicit models are presented in

with population dynamics in a fitness landscape (as described by simple theoretical models of biological evolution).

We have applied our theoretical frameworks to two different explicit microscopic models to illustrate several important
outcomes of our work, yielding a satisfactory and qualitative (or in some cases even quantitative) agreement between
agent-based simulations and theoretical predictions. Starting from a simple example of the AOUP model of active
particles coupled to an external field, we have first considered the basic case when the reward encodes the optimization

## Answer: "Markov chain model" across the corpus

No single paper in this ~100-document corpus is *about* Markov chain models as its subject. The concept appears in three distinct roles, and it's worth separating them because most matches are the term "Markov chain" used for a *sampling method* (MCMC), not for a *model*. Here is the complete picture, cited by document and page.

### 1. Markov chain used as the actual model — the strongest, most direct hit
**`1606.06090.pdf`** (population genetics; conditioned selection inference). This paper builds its analysis *on* a Markov chain model:

- The count of type-B alleles, N_B, is "described as a **Markov chain in discrete time with two absorbing states** in N_B = 0 and N_B = N," the two absorbing states corresponding to fixation of allele A and of allele B respectively (**page 3**).
- Two concrete instantiations of this Markov chain are studied: the **Moran model** (haploid, overlapping generations) and the **Wright–Fisher model** (diploid, non-overlapping generations). The Wright–Fisher chain "is numerically more challenging than the Moran model" because its time-to-fixation is shorter; transition probabilities of the chain are used to derive conditional and unconditioned likelihoods of the selection coefficient (**page 8**).
- A related reference is cited: Zhao, Lascoux & Waxman, "An informational transition in **conditioned Markov chains**" (**page 13**).

This is the one document where "Markov chain model" is literally the object of study.

### 2. Markov structure as a modeling device / embedding
**`2607.02154.pdf`** — *Path-Measure Dynamics of Attention-Driven World Models*. Here a Markov construction is the mechanism, not the sampler:

- It constructs "the **minimal exact mechanism**… not a nonlocal dynamics posited directly, but a **Markovian one** for the observed z ∈ ℝᵈ coupled to a hidden auxiliary field w" (**page 3**).
- The non-Markovian memory induced by attention is shown to be "the **projection of a hidden linear Markov augmentation**"; eliminating the auxiliary field yields a nonlocal Onsager–Machlup action, and the kernels "exactly match a **hidden Markov embedding** with a finite relaxation spectrum" (**pages 1, 4**).

### 3. Markov chains named as background lineage
**`2312.00752.pdf`** (Mamba / selective state space models). In surveying what "state space model" has meant across fields, it lists "**Markov decision processes (MDP)**… **hidden Markov models (HMM)** and linear dynamical systems (LDS)" as prior recurrent-latent-state concepts (**page 4**). It does not itself build a Markov chain model.

### 4. "Markov chain" as a *method* (MCMC), not a model — for completeness
Most remaining corpus matches are Markov chain **Monte Carlo** used as an inference/sampling tool. These are *not* Markov chain models:

- **`1302.4245.pdf`** (Gaussian-process kernels): MCMC to integrate out GP hyperparameters (**pages 3, 9**).
- **`2607.06755.pdf`** (galaxy gravity/anisotropy): posterior sampled with the emcee affine-invariant MCMC sampler (**page 12**).
- **`2607.06844.pdf`** (ultra-fast outflows): parameter uncertainties via MCMC line fitting (**page 6**).
- **`0802.0733.pdf`** (airplane boarding): MCMC *optimization* of boarding order (**page 1**).
- **`1501.05624.pdf`**: cites Bayesian probabilistic matrix factorization "using Markov chain Monte Carlo" (**page 10**).
- **`0707.4042.pdf`**: cites the textbook Keilson, *Markov Chain Models — Rarity and Exponentiality* as a reference only (**page 15**).
- **`2607.08291.pdf`** (market making): reference list mentions "data uncertainty in **markov chains**" and "robust **markov decision processes**" (**page 32**) — bibliographic, not a model used in the work.

**Bottom line:** if the question means a genuine *Markov chain model*, the answer is `1606.06090.pdf` (allele-frequency dynamics as a discrete-time Markov chain with absorbing fixation states, realized as the Moran and Wright–Fisher models; pages 3 and 8), with a secondary, more abstract use of a hidden-Markov embedding in `2607.02154.pdf` (pages 1–4). Everything else in the corpus is either background terminology (`2312.00752.pdf`, p. 4) or MCMC-as-a-sampling-method, which is a different thing.
